title: A time for everything (Ecclesiastes 3:1–8)
hook: a time to be born, to die, to weep, to laugh, to keep silence

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Preacher's first word, hevel, and your line was all is breath. What did you let pass? Day four hundred fifty-five.

You may know this passage without knowing you know it. It's read at funerals. It's read at weddings. In 1965 a rock band took it to the top of the American charts, in a song Pete Seeger had set almost word for word from the King James Bible, adding only a refrain and a few words at the end. And it comes from Ecclesiastes, from the same Preacher who just told us that everything is breath. Today, his list of times.
screen: `READ AT FUNERALS AND WEDDINGS.` → `A NUMBER-ONE SONG IN 1965.` → `FROM THE PREACHER OF BREATH.`

segments.voice: It starts with a heading: "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Then the list, in pairs. "A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted." A time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance. And a line for every hard conversation: "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak." Count them and there are fourteen pairs, twenty-eight times, and every pair holds two opposites. That's the shape of a life. Not one long mood, but a back and forth. Notice what the Preacher doesn't do. He isn't telling you to pick the nice half. He doesn't say avoid weeping, aim for laughing. He says both have their time. Grief isn't a failure of joy. Silence isn't a failure of speech. The question is never which feeling is right, but which time it is now. Readers have heard this in two keys. For some, it's comfort: whatever you're going through, it's a season, and seasons turn. For others it's sobering, because the Preacher goes straight on to ask what anyone gains from all this toil, since the times come whether we like them or not. Then he adds a strange line. The King James says God has set the world in their heart; the Hebrew word, olam, can also mean the everlasting. And yet, he says, no one can find out the whole of what God has done. We live inside the seasons. We can't see the whole calendar. This week we've walked from Job's ending through the wisdom books: wisdom's beginning, the ant, rakh, eshet chayil, all is breath. Today, a time for everything.
screen: `TO EVERY THING THERE IS A SEASON.` · `FOURTEEN PAIRS OF OPPOSITES.` · `BOTH HALVES HAVE THEIR TIME.` · `THE EVERLASTING SET IN THE HEART.` · then, large: `A TIME TO KEEP SILENCE, AND A TIME TO SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name what time it is for you. Settle, and breathe. Let the list play slowly through your mind. A time to plant, a time to pluck up. A time to weep, a time to laugh. A time to keep silence, a time to speak. Which line catches? Don't pick the one you wish were true. Pick the one that is. Say it to yourself plainly: it's a time to mourn, or it's a time to build. Then simply let it be the season it is. If you pray, you can offer that season to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Et. Hebrew for a fitting moment, repeated twenty-eight times in the Preacher's list of fourteen pairs: every season of a life, the hard half and the easy half, each in its time.
Your line: a time to speak. Today, before you speak in a hard moment, ask yourself one quiet question: is this a time to keep silence, or a time to speak? Day four hundred fifty-five.

screen: `DAY 455 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWO ARE BETTER THAN ONE.`

howItsDone: Ecclesiastes 3:1–8 is often read at Christian funerals, and it is also read at weddings, graduations and memorial services, often by a family member.

fork.setup: you're in a season of grief. a friend tells you it's time to cheer up. what does the Preacher's list say?
options: your friend is right: laughing is better than weeping.
there is a time to mourn, and this may be it.
fork.reveal: "a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance." the list never ranks the halves. each has its season, and seasons turn.

original.note: Hebrew: a time, a fitting moment. it appears twenty-eight times in the list.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle poem for funerals and weddings.
what it means: life comes in opposite seasons, and both halves of each pair have their time.
what a scholar hears: twenty-eight uses of et, a fitting time, in fourteen pairs, then 3:11: God has set olam, eternity or the sense of time, in the human heart.

notes: Audit (y2 second sample): the hook repeated day 454's exact line 'the most unsettling book in the Bible'; removed it, the vague 'rooms full of people... recognize it by the second line', and the superlative 'one of the most practical lines in the Bible'. The 3:11 paraphrase ('God has set eternity in the human heart') echoed a modern copyrighted translation; now gives the KJV sense ('the world') and the Hebrew olam. Trapdoor's 'everything happens for a reason' repeated day 445's hook and practice; replaced.

Pete Seeger's 'Turn! Turn! Turn!' (written late 1950s) was a US number-one hit for the Byrds in late 1965; Seeger added the refrain and the closing words. Confirm the hook's phrasing; no lyrics are quoted.

Ecclesiastes 3:11 is paraphrased (KJV: 'he hath set the world in their heart'). The Hebrew olam is rendered 'eternity' in many modern versions and 'the world' in the KJV; the trapdoor names both senses. Confirm.
